Intelligent Disaster Detection from Social Media Using Word2Vec, RNN and LSTM¶
Name Riyan Khan Durrani
Reg.no 2023611
Course AI451-L (NLP LAB)
Assessment NLP Lab Mid – Question # 03 (CLO-2, GA-5) P4 – 20 marks
Dataset Natural Language Processing with Disaster Tweets (Kaggle) – labelled train.csv, 7,613 tweets

Goal. Distinguish tweets that describe a real disaster (target = 1) from tweets that merely use disaster words figuratively or in another context (target = 0), using a self-trained 100-d Word2Vec embedding feeding a Simple RNN and an LSTM classifier.

Task Marks Section
Q3.1 Preprocessing pipeline (clean, tokenize, encode, pad, 80:20 stratified split) 5 Q3.1
Q3.2 100-d Word2Vec + PCA visualisation of 10 words 5 Q3.2
Q3.3 Simple RNN and LSTM with the Word2Vec embeddings, identical settings (≤ 5 epochs) 5 Q3.3
Q3.4 Evaluation: accuracy / precision / recall / F1, confusion matrices, loss plots 2.5 Q3.4
Q3.5 Error analysis of two misclassified tweets + one justified improvement 2.5 Q3.5
Total 20

Design principles used throughout

  • No leakage. Every fitted component (vocabulary, Word2Vec, padding length) is fitted on the training tweets only; the 20 % test set is touched once, at evaluation time.
  • Fair comparison. Both networks share the same embedding matrix, architecture skeleton, optimiser, batch size, epoch budget, callbacks, seed and data splits – the recurrent cell is the only difference.
  • Reproducible. Fixed seeds, deterministic TensorFlow ops, single-threaded Word2Vec with a deterministic hash function. Re-running the notebook on the same library versions gives identical numbers.

Runs as-is on Google Colab (Runtime → Run all, ≈ 8 minutes on the free CPU runtime, no GPU needed): the dataset is fetched and validated automatically, and every dependency is pre-installed on Colab (a guard cell installs gensim if missing).

1. Dataset and quick exploratory analysis¶

The Kaggle page requires a login, so the loader tries, in order: a local copy (data/train.csv, Kaggle input folder), an automatic download of a public copy of the competition's train.csv, and finally an upload prompt (Colab). Whatever is found is validated (7,613 rows, expected columns, 3,271 disaster / 4,342 non-disaster labels).

In [3]:
import urllib.request

EXPECTED_COLS = ["id", "keyword", "location", "text", "target"]
MIRROR_URL = ("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tarunannapareddy/"
              "Natural-Language-Processing-with-Disaster-Tweets/main/train.csv")
CANDIDATES = [Path("data/train.csv"), Path("train.csv"),
              Path("/kaggle/input/nlp-getting-started/train.csv"), Path("/content/train.csv")]


def is_valid_train_csv(path) -> bool:
    try:
        d = pd.read_csv(path)
        return (d.shape == (7613, 5) and list(d.columns) == EXPECTED_COLS
                and d["target"].value_counts().to_dict() == {0: 4342, 1: 3271})
    except Exception:
        return False


def locate_train_csv() -> Path:
    for p in CANDIDATES:                                                     # 1) local copy
        if p.exists() and is_valid_train_csv(p):
            return p
    target = Path("data/train.csv")                                          # 2) public copy of the Kaggle file
    try:
        target.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(MIRROR_URL, target)
        if is_valid_train_csv(target):
            return target
        print("Downloaded file failed validation.")
    except Exception as exc:
        print(f"Automatic download failed ({type(exc).__name__}: {exc}).")
    try:                                                                     # 3) Colab upload prompt
        from google.colab import files
        print("Please upload train.csv (Kaggle: nlp-getting-started).")
        for name in files.upload():
            if is_valid_train_csv(name):
                return Path(name)
    except ImportError:
        pass
    raise FileNotFoundError("train.csv not found - put the Kaggle nlp-getting-started train.csv in ./data/")

Observations. The classes are mildly imbalanced (4,342 non-disaster vs 3,271 disaster, i.e. 43 % disaster), so accuracy alone is not enough – precision, recall and F1 of the disaster class are reported alongside it. keyword (61 missing) and location (2,533 missing) are not used: the task defines text as the input and target as the label. A few tweets are exact duplicates (110 extra rows, 18 duplicated texts with conflicting labels); they are kept to stay faithful to the 7,613-tweet dataset, and their effect on the test set is quantified in Q3.1 and in the robustness checks of Q3.4.

Q3.1 Preprocessing pipeline (5 marks)¶

Pipeline – raw tweet → clean → tokenize → stratified 80:20 split → vocabulary → integer encoding → padding

Step Decision and justification
Clean lower-case; decode HTML entities (&amp;); remove URLs and @mentions (no topical signal, would pollute the vocabulary); keep the word of a #hashtag (#earthquake is highly informative); drop digits, punctuation and non-ASCII noise
Tokenize regex [a-z]+(?:'[a-z]+)* – keeps contractions (don't), discards dangling quote marks
Stop-words kept – negations and function words matter for sequence models, and Word2Vec uses them as context
Split stratified 80:20 (random_state=42) so both parts keep the 43/57 class ratio
Vocabulary built from training tweets only; words seen fewer than min_count = 2 times map to <OOV> (same threshold as Word2Vec, so the two vocabularies coincide)
Padding maxlen = 95th percentile of training lengths (computed on train only); pre-padding, post-truncation; index 0 is <PAD> and is masked inside the recurrent layers

Cleaning/tokenising is stateless, so it is applied to all tweets before the split; everything that is learned from data (vocabulary, Word2Vec, maxlen) is fitted after the split on the training part only.

In [4]:
URL_RE = re.compile(r"https?://\S+|www\.\S+")
MENTION_RE = re.compile(r"@\w+")
TOKEN_RE = re.compile(r"[a-z]+(?:'[a-z]+)*")


def clean_text(text: str) -> str:
    """Lower-case, strip URLs/mentions/hashtag symbols/digits/punctuation, normalise whitespace."""
    text = html.unescape(text).lower()
    text = URL_RE.sub(" ", text)
    text = MENTION_RE.sub(" ", text)
    text = text.replace("#", " ")                 # keep the hashtag word itself
    text = re.sub(r"[^a-z'\s]", " ", text)       # digits, punctuation, emoji, non-ASCII
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()


def tokenize(clean: str) -> list:
    return TOKEN_RE.findall(clean)


df["clean"] = df["text"].map(clean_text)
df["tokens"] = df["clean"].map(tokenize)
assert (df["tokens"].map(len) > 0).all(), "a tweet became empty after cleaning"

# ---- vocabulary (training tweets only) -> integer encoding -> padding
PAD, OOV = 0, 1
word_counts = Counter(tok for toks in train_df["tokens"] for tok in toks)
vocab_words = sorted((w for w, c in word_counts.items() if c >= W2V_MIN_COUNT), key=lambda w: (-word_counts[w], w))
word2idx = {w: i + 2 for i, w in enumerate(vocab_words)}                  # 0 = <PAD>, 1 = <OOV>
idx2word = {0: "<PAD>", 1: "<OOV>", **{i: w for w, i in word2idx.items()}}

train_lens = train_df["tokens"].map(len)
MAX_LEN = int(np.ceil(np.percentile(train_lens, 95)))                      # fitted on train only


def encode_pad(token_lists):
    seqs = [[word2idx.get(tok, OOV) for tok in toks] for toks in token_lists]
    return keras.utils.pad_sequences(seqs, maxlen=MAX_LEN, padding="pre", truncating="post", value=PAD)


X_train_all, y_train_all = encode_pad(train_df["tokens"]), train_df["target"].to_numpy()
X_test, y_test = encode_pad(test_df["tokens"]), test_df["target"].to_numpy()

# validation part carved out of the training part (used for loss curves + early stopping, never the test set)
tr_idx, val_idx = train_test_split(np.arange(len(train_df)), test_size=VAL_SIZE, stratify=y_train_all,
                                   random_state=SEED)
X_tr, y_tr, X_val, y_val = X_train_all[tr_idx], y_train_all[tr_idx], X_train_all[val_idx], y_train_all[val_idx]

print(f"Vocabulary (min_count={W2V_MIN_COUNT}): {len(vocab_words):,} words + <PAD> + <OOV> = {len(idx2word):,} indices")
print(f"MAX_LEN = {MAX_LEN} (95th pct of train lengths; longest train tweet = {train_lens.max()} tokens; "
      f"{(train_lens > MAX_LEN).mean():.1%} of train tweets get truncated)")
print(f"X_tr {X_tr.shape} | X_val {X_val.shape} | X_test {X_test.shape}  (dtype {X_tr.dtype})")
print(f"Disaster share  train {y_tr.mean():.3f} | val {y_val.mean():.3f} | test {y_test.mean():.3f}")
oov_rate = np.mean([word2idx.get(tok, OOV) == OOV for toks in test_df["tokens"] for tok in toks])
print(f"Share of test tokens that are <OOV> (unseen / rare in training): {oov_rate:.1%}")

What the output shows

  • Stratified split: 6,090 training / 1,523 test tweets; the disaster share is 42.97 % vs 42.94 % – the class ratio is preserved, and the validation part (609 tweets) carved from the training part keeps it too (0.430).
  • Vocabulary: 5,547 words seen at least twice in the training tweets, plus <PAD> (0) and <OOV> (1) = 5,549 indices.
  • Padding length: MAX_LEN = 24 (95th percentile of training lengths; the longest training tweet has 32 tokens), so only 3.4 % of training tweets are truncated while very little padding is wasted. Padding is pre, truncation post.
  • Generalisation gap: 12.6 % of the test tokens are <OOV> (rare or unseen in the training tweets) – a limitation of learning embeddings from only 6,090 tweets that is revisited in Q3.5.
  • Leakage caveat: 231 test tweets (15.2 %) have a cleaned text identical to a training tweet (retweets / copy-paste). They are kept for fidelity to the dataset; Q3.4 re-evaluates both models without them.

Q3.2 100-dimensional Word2Vec and PCA visualisation (5 marks)¶

Word2Vec is trained from scratch on the 6,090 training tweets (no labels, no test tweets, no pre-trained vectors). Skip-gram with negative sampling is used because it models rare words better than CBOW on a small corpus (~80 k tokens); window = 5, min_count = 2, 50 epochs to compensate for the small corpus, a single worker and a deterministic hash function so the result is reproducible.

In [7]:
def stable_hash(s: str) -> int:        # gensim's default hash() is salted per process -> not reproducible
    return zlib.crc32(s.encode("utf-8"))


t0 = time.time()
w2v = Word2Vec(sentences=train_df["tokens"].tolist(), vector_size=W2V_DIM, window=W2V_WINDOW,
               min_count=W2V_MIN_COUNT, sg=1, negative=10, epochs=W2V_EPOCHS,
               seed=SEED, workers=1, hashfxn=stable_hash)
print(f"Word2Vec trained in {time.time() - t0:.1f}s | vector size {w2v.vector_size} | "
      f"vocabulary {len(w2v.wv):,} | corpus tokens {w2v.corpus_total_words:,}")
assert w2v.vector_size == 100
assert set(w2v.wv.index_to_key) == set(vocab_words), "Word2Vec and encoder vocabularies must coincide"

# embedding matrix aligned with the integer encoding: row 0 = <PAD>, row 1 = <OOV> (both zero vectors)
embedding_matrix = np.zeros((len(idx2word), W2V_DIM), dtype="float32")
for word, idx in word2idx.items():
    embedding_matrix[idx] = w2v.wv[word]
print("Embedding matrix:", embedding_matrix.shape)
w2v.wv.save(str(OUT_DIR / "word2vec_100d.kv"))

# Selection rule: 4 disaster hazards, 3 harm/response words and 3 everyday words, each occurring >= 40 times in the
# training tweets so that its vector rests on enough contexts (very rare words have unreliable vectors).
SELECTED = ["fire", "flood", "earthquake", "storm", "killed", "emergency", "police", "love", "good", "school"]
GROUP = {"fire": "hazard", "flood": "hazard", "earthquake": "hazard", "storm": "hazard",
         "killed": "harm / response", "emergency": "harm / response", "police": "harm / response",
         "love": "everyday", "good": "everyday", "school": "everyday"}
missing = [w for w in SELECTED if w not in w2v.wv]
assert not missing, f"not in vocabulary: {missing}"
assert all(word_counts[w] >= 40 for w in SELECTED), {w: word_counts[w] for w in SELECTED}

                                      for w in SELECTED]})

vecs = np.vstack([w2v.wv[w] for w in SELECTED])
pca = PCA(n_components=2, random_state=SEED).fit(vecs)
xy = pca.transform(vecs)
evr = pca.explained_variance_ratio_
print(f"PCA explained variance: PC1 {evr[0]:.1%}, PC2 {evr[1]:.1%}  (total {evr.sum():.1%})")

unit = vecs / np.linalg.norm(vecs, axis=1, keepdims=True)
sim = pd.DataFrame(unit @ unit.T, index=SELECTED, columns=SELECTED)      # cosine similarity matrix
assert np.isclose(sim.loc["fire", "flood"], w2v.wv.similarity("fire", "flood"), atol=1e-5)

palette = {"hazard": "#c0392b", "harm / response": "#2a6fbb", "everyday": "#2e8b57"}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5.6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.15, 1]})
for (word, (x, y)) in zip(SELECTED, xy):
    ax[0].scatter(x, y, s=120, color=palette[GROUP[word]], edgecolor="white", zorder=3)
    ax[0].annotate(word, (x, y), xytext=(7, 6), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=11)
ax[0].axhline(0, color="#ccc", lw=0.8); ax[0].axvline(0, color="#ccc", lw=0.8)
ax[0].set(title="PCA of 10 selected Word2Vec embeddings (100-d -> 2-d)",
          xlabel=f"PC1 ({evr[0]:.1%} variance)", ylabel=f"PC2 ({evr[1]:.1%} variance)")
handles = [plt.Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=c, label=g) for g, c in palette.items()]
ax[0].legend(handles=handles, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.14), ncol=3, frameon=False,
             title="semantic group (assigned by hand)")
sns.heatmap(sim, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="vlag", center=0, vmin=-1, vmax=1, square=True,
            cbar_kws={"label": "cosine similarity", "shrink": 0.8}, annot_kws={"size": 8}, ax=ax[1])
ax[1].set_title("Cosine similarity between the same words")
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig(fig, "02_word2vec_pca.png"); plt.show()

pair_sims = {(a, b): sim.loc[a, b] for i, a in enumerate(SELECTED) for b in SELECTED[i + 1:]}     # 45 unique pairs
ranked = sorted(pair_sims.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])
print("Most similar pairs :", "; ".join(f"{a}-{b} {v:.2f}" for (a, b), v in ranked[:5]))
print("Least similar pairs:", "; ".join(f"{a}-{b} {v:.2f}" for (a, b), v in ranked[-5:]))
within = np.mean([v for (a, b), v in pair_sims.items() if GROUP[a] == GROUP[b]])
between = np.mean([v for (a, b), v in pair_sims.items() if GROUP[a] != GROUP[b]])
print(f"Mean cosine within hand-made groups {within:.3f} vs between groups {between:.3f}  "
      f"({sum(GROUP[a] == GROUP[b] for a, b in pair_sims)} within-pairs, {sum(GROUP[a] != GROUP[b] for a, b in pair_sims)} between-pairs)")

# does the geometry reflect real co-occurrence in the tweets?  (skip-gram places words that share contexts close together)
tok_sets = [set(toks) for toks in train_df["tokens"]]
co_rows = []
for (a, b), v in ranked[:4] + ranked[-2:]:
    na, nb_ = sum(a in ts for ts in tok_sets), sum(b in ts for ts in tok_sets)
    co_rows.append(dict(pair=f"{a} - {b}", cosine=round(v, 2), tweets_with_first=na, tweets_with_second=nb_,
                        together=sum(a in ts and b in ts for ts in tok_sets),
                        expected_if_independent=round(na * nb_ / len(tok_sets), 2)))
display(pd.DataFrame(co_rows).style.hide(axis="index"))

Least similar pairs: storm-love 0.04; police-love 0.03; storm-school 0.03; love-school 0.01; fire-love -0.02

killed - police 0.340000 80 109 13 1.430000
fire - school 0.310000 188 47 1 1.450000
flood - killed 0.260000 49 80 4 0.640000

Interpretation (read from the PCA plot and the cosine-similarity matrix above)

  • How much to trust the picture. The two principal components retain only 29.5 % of the variance (PC1 15.5 %, PC2 14.0 %), so the 2-D map is a rough shadow of the 100-d space; the cosine matrix on the right is used to cross-check every statement.
  • The one strong, explainable relationship: killed – police (cosine 0.34, the highest of the 45 pairs). The two words co-occur in 13 training tweets where only 1.4 would be expected by chance (≈ 9×) – shootings, arrests and attacks in news tweets – and on the plot both lie on the right-hand side (PC1 ≈ 2–3). flood – killed (0.26; together in 4 tweets vs 0.6 expected) is the same effect: flood-casualty reports. Skip-gram puts words that share contexts close together, and these are the contexts of tragic news.
  • The hazard words do not form a tight cluster. fire, flood, earthquake, storm are scattered across both components; their mean similarity to each other is low (0.13–0.20 per pair) and the mean cosine within my hand-made groups (0.164) is barely above the mean between groups (0.152). earthquake in particular sits far from everything (all cosines ≤ 0.21): its tweets share a narrow template (magnitude, place, time), so its vector is dominated by that template rather than by general disaster vocabulary.
  • Everyday words are not close to each other either (love – school 0.01) – but love is the most isolated word, with the lowest similarity to fire (−0.02), school (0.01), police (0.03) and storm (0.04): the only clear "everyday vs. disaster" signal in the map.
  • Spurious pair. fire – school has cosine 0.31 although the two words appear together in just 1 tweet (1.45 expected): the vectors are close through shared neighbours, not through direct co-occurrence – a sign of noise typical of a corpus of only ≈ 83 k tokens.

Take-away. The self-trained Word2Vec space captures topical co-occurrence in disaster news (killed/police/flood) but not a clean semantic taxonomy, because most selected words occur only 40–210 times. This is enough to give the classifiers a useful signal, but it is a weak representation – the observation that motivates the improvement proposed in Q3.5.

Q3.3 Simple RNN and LSTM with the Word2Vec embeddings (5 marks)¶

Both models use exactly the same recipe; only the recurrent cell changes.

Input (MAX_LEN) -> Embedding(100-d, Word2Vec weights, frozen, mask_zero) -> {SimpleRNN | LSTM}(64)
                -> Dropout(0.3) -> Dense(32, ReLU) -> Dropout(0.3) -> Dense(1, sigmoid)
Setting Value (identical for both)
Embedding trained Word2Vec matrix, frozen so the comparison measures the recurrent cell on top of the same fixed features
Optimiser / loss Adam (lr = 1e-3) / binary cross-entropy
Batch size / epochs 32 / at most 5
Early stopping monitor val_loss, patience 2, restore best weights
Data same X_tr (5,481) / X_val (609) split, same seed before each build
In [10]:
def build_model(kind: str, matrix: np.ndarray = embedding_matrix) -> keras.Model:
    cell = {"SimpleRNN": keras.layers.SimpleRNN, "LSTM": keras.layers.LSTM}[kind]
    model = keras.Sequential([
        keras.Input(shape=(MAX_LEN,), dtype="int32"),
        keras.layers.Embedding(matrix.shape[0], matrix.shape[1], mask_zero=True, trainable=False,
                               name="word2vec_embedding"),
        cell(RNN_UNITS, name=kind.lower()),
        keras.layers.Dropout(DROPOUT),
        keras.layers.Dense(32, activation="relu"),
        keras.layers.Dropout(DROPOUT),
        keras.layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid"),
    ], name=f"{kind}_classifier")
    model.get_layer("word2vec_embedding").set_weights([matrix])
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(model.get_layer("word2vec_embedding").get_weights()[0], matrix)
    model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(LR), loss="binary_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
    return model


def train_model(kind: str, seed: int = SEED, matrix: np.ndarray = embedding_matrix,
                data=None, verbose: int = 2):
    """Train one classifier with the shared recipe. `data` = (X_tr, y_tr, X_val, y_val); default = Word2Vec encoding."""
    Xa, ya, Xv, yv = data if data is not None else (X_tr, y_tr, X_val, y_val)
    keras.utils.set_random_seed(seed)                 # identical RNG state for both models
    model = build_model(kind, matrix)
    stopper = keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", patience=2, restore_best_weights=True)
    t0 = time.time()
    hist = model.fit(Xa, ya, validation_data=(Xv, yv), epochs=MAX_EPOCHS, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE,
                     shuffle=True, callbacks=[stopper], verbose=verbose)
    return model, hist.history, time.time() - t0


models, histories, fit_seconds = {}, {}, {}
for kind in ["SimpleRNN", "LSTM"]:
    print(f"\n{'=' * 20} {kind} {'=' * 20}")
    models[kind], histories[kind], fit_seconds[kind] = train_model(kind)
    assert len(histories[kind]["loss"]) <= MAX_EPOCHS
    models[kind].summary()

What the output shows. Both models were built with the same recipe and the same frozen 100-d Word2Vec matrix (554,900 frozen parameters each); the settings table above is read back from the trained objects and the notebook asserts that they match. The SimpleRNN has 12,673 trainable parameters, the LSTM 44,353 (its four gates make it ≈ 3.5× larger). Neither model exceeded the 5-epoch limit: the SimpleRNN used all 5 epochs (best validation loss at epoch 5) while the LSTM stopped after 4 epochs because early stopping found no validation improvement after epoch 2, and the epoch-2 weights were restored.

Q3.4 Evaluation and comparison (2.5 marks)¶

All numbers below are computed on the held-out 20 % test set (1,523 tweets) with the best-validation weights. Precision / recall / F1 are for the positive (disaster) class; macro-F1 averages both classes.

In [12]:
def evaluate(kind: str) -> dict:
    prob = models[kind].predict(X_test, batch_size=256, verbose=0).ravel()
    pred = (prob >= 0.5).astype(int)
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, pred, labels=[0, 1])
    tn, fp, fn, tp = cm.ravel()
    # independent cross-check of sklearn from the confusion matrix
    assert np.isclose(accuracy_score(y_test, pred), (tp + tn) / cm.sum())
    assert np.isclose(precision_score(y_test, pred), tp / (tp + fp))
    assert np.isclose(recall_score(y_test, pred), tp / (tp + fn))
    return dict(prob=prob, pred=pred, cm=cm,
                Accuracy=accuracy_score(y_test, pred), Precision=precision_score(y_test, pred),
                Recall=recall_score(y_test, pred), F1=f1_score(y_test, pred),
                MacroF1=f1_score(y_test, pred, average="macro"), AUC=roc_auc_score(y_test, prob))


results = {k: evaluate(k) for k in models}

                      for k in results}).T
table.columns = ["Accuracy", "Precision", "Recall", "F1-score", "Macro-F1", "ROC-AUC"]
table["Epochs run"] = [len(histories[k]["loss"]) for k in table.index]
table["Best epoch"] = [int(np.argmin(histories[k]["val_loss"])) + 1 for k in table.index]
table["Trainable params"] = [int(sum(np.prod(w.shape) for w in models[k].trainable_weights)) for k in table.index]
table["Fit time (s)"] = [round(fit_seconds[k], 1) for k in table.index]

    subset=table.columns[:6], color="#d6efd8"))

    print(classification_report(y_test, results[k]["pred"], target_names=["Non-disaster (0)", "Disaster (1)"], digits=4))

                   "epochs_run": len(histories[k]["loss"]),
                   "history": {m: [float(x) for x in v] for m, v in histories[k].items()}} for k in results},
    "mcnemar": {"only_rnn_correct": b, "only_lstm_correct": c, "p_value": float(p_mcnemar)},
}
(OUT_DIR / "metrics.json").write_text(json.dumps(metrics_json, indent=2))
print("Saved outputs/metrics.json and outputs/test_predictions.csv")

Saved outputs/metrics.json and outputs/test_predictions.csv

Robustness checks (extra, do not change the headline numbers above)¶

A single run on a single split can mislead, so two sanity checks are added:

  1. Seed variance – both models are retrained with five further seeds (same data, same Word2Vec matrix, same recipe).
  2. Duplicate-free test set – the headline metrics are recomputed on test tweets whose cleaned text does not also occur in the training set (removes the leakage caveat from Q3.1).
In [15]:
# 1) seed variance
SEEDS = [11, 22, 33, 44, 55]
rows = []
for seed in SEEDS:
    for kind in ["SimpleRNN", "LSTM"]:
        m, h, _ = train_model(kind, seed=seed, verbose=0)
        p = (m.predict(X_test, batch_size=256, verbose=0).ravel() >= 0.5).astype(int)
        rows.append(dict(seed=seed, model=kind, Accuracy=accuracy_score(y_test, p), Precision=precision_score(y_test, p),
                         Recall=recall_score(y_test, p), F1=f1_score(y_test, p), epochs=len(h["loss"])))
seed_df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
agg = seed_df.groupby("model")[["Accuracy", "Precision", "Recall", "F1"]].agg(["mean", "std"]).round(4)
display(agg)
piv = seed_df.pivot(index="seed", columns="model", values="F1")
print(f"LSTM F1 > SimpleRNN F1 in {(piv['LSTM'] > piv['SimpleRNN']).sum()} of {len(SEEDS)} seeds "
      f"(mean paired difference {(piv['LSTM'] - piv['SimpleRNN']).mean():+.4f})")

# 2) duplicate-free test subset

dedup = pd.DataFrame({k: dict(Accuracy=accuracy_score(y_test[mask], results[k]["pred"][mask]),
                              Precision=precision_score(y_test[mask], results[k]["pred"][mask]),
                              Recall=recall_score(y_test[mask], results[k]["pred"][mask]),
                              F1=f1_score(y_test[mask], results[k]["pred"][mask])) for k in results}).T
print(f"\nTest tweets not seen verbatim in training: {mask.sum()} of {len(mask)}")
display(dedup.round(4))
seed_df.to_csv(OUT_DIR / "seed_robustness.csv", index=False)

Comparison of the two models¶

Test set (1,523 tweets) Accuracy Precision Recall F1 ROC-AUC
Simple RNN 0.7965 0.8346 0.6560 0.7346 0.8460
LSTM 0.8070 0.8346 0.6865 0.7534 0.8583
  • The LSTM is ahead, modestly. Compared with the Simple RNN it gains +1.05 points of accuracy, +3.05 of recall, +1.88 of F1 and +0.012 of AUC; precision is tied (0.8346). The confusion matrices show where it comes from: the LSTM recovers 20 more genuine disaster tweets (449 vs 429 true positives; false negatives 205 vs 225) at the price of 4 more false alarms (89 vs 85 false positives).
  • Both models are cautious. Precision is high (≈ 0.83) but recall is only 0.66–0.69: about one disaster tweet in three is missed (false-negative rate 34.4 % / 31.3 %) while only ≈ 10 % of non-disaster tweets raise a false alarm. Disaster tweets are the minority class (43 %), and many of them are phrased casually, so the 0.5 threshold favours the majority class.
  • Loss curves. Simple RNN: validation loss falls from 0.516 to 0.490 and is still creeping down at epoch 5 (training loss 0.453) – it is only mildly over-fitted and would probably profit from a few more epochs, which the 5-epoch cap forbids. LSTM: validation loss is lowest at epoch 2 (0.479), then rises (0.489 at epoch 3) while training loss keeps dropping to 0.433 – it starts over-fitting from epoch 3 because its larger capacity memorises the training tweets faster; early stopping with weight restoration protects the final model. The LSTM's best validation loss (0.479) is lower than the Simple RNN's (0.490).
  • How reliable is the gap? An exact McNemar test on the discordant predictions (45 tweets only the RNN got right, 61 only the LSTM) gives p = 0.145, i.e. not significant at 5 %. Over five additional seeds the LSTM's mean accuracy is again higher (0.7886 ± 0.0111 vs 0.7782 ± 0.0101), but the mean F1 gap shrinks to +0.4 points (0.7132 vs 0.7096, LSTM ahead in 3 of 5 seeds, seed-to-seed standard deviation ≈ 3 points). On the 1,292 test tweets that never appear verbatim in the training set, the LSTM still leads (accuracy 0.8003 vs 0.7848, F1 0.7177 vs 0.6904), and both models score slightly lower than on the full set – the duplicates inflated the headline numbers a little.
  • Verdict. The LSTM is the better and more consistent model on this task (higher accuracy, recall, F1 and AUC in the main run, higher mean accuracy over seeds), as expected from its gating mechanism, which mitigates the vanishing-gradient problem of the plain RNN. The advantage is small because tweets are short (median 13 tokens) and the frozen embeddings are the real bottleneck; with a single split it cannot be called statistically significant.

Q3.5 Error analysis and one justified improvement (2.5 marks)¶

The analysis uses the better model (higher test F1). To avoid cherry-picking, the two tweets are selected by a fixed rule: the most confidently wrong false positive and the most confidently wrong false negative of that model.

In [16]:
best_kind = table["F1-score"].idxmax()
err = test_out.assign(p_best=results[best_kind]["prob"], pred_best=results[best_kind]["pred"],
                      clean=test_df["clean"].values, tokens=test_df["tokens"].values)
err = err[err["pred_best"] != err["y_true"]].copy()
err["confidence_in_wrong_label"] = np.where(err["pred_best"] == 1, err["p_best"], 1 - err["p_best"])

# Some "errors" are not model failures: the same cleaned text occurs in the dataset with BOTH labels, so the ground
# truth is undefined. They are counted and excluded from the selection so the two analysed tweets are real mistakes.
label_sets = df.groupby("clean")["target"].nunique()
conflicting_texts = set(label_sets[label_sets > 1].index)
err["label_conflict"] = err["clean"].isin(conflicting_texts)
n_fp, n_fn = int((err.y_true == 0).sum()), int((err.y_true == 1).sum())
print(f"Best model: {best_kind} | errors on test set: {len(err)} (FP {n_fp}, FN {n_fn}) | "
      f"errors whose text carries conflicting labels elsewhere in the data: {int(err.label_conflict.sum())}")
clean_err = err[~err["label_conflict"]]
fp_row = clean_err[clean_err.y_true == 0].sort_values("confidence_in_wrong_label", ascending=False).iloc[0]
fn_row = clean_err[clean_err.y_true == 1].sort_values("confidence_in_wrong_label", ascending=False).iloc[0]
print("Selection rule: most confidently wrong false positive / false negative among errors with unambiguous labels.\n")

Analysis of the two errors¶

Error 1 – false positive (id 8637, keyword seismic). "ENGLAND EAST COAST. Dogger Bank Westward. 1. Seismic survey in progress by M/V Western Regent towing a 8400 metre long cable within area…" – a maritime notice about geophysical exploration (a vessel towing a survey cable), labelled non-disaster, yet the LSTM says "disaster" with P = 0.990 (Simple RNN 0.950). Likely reasons:

  1. Lexical shortcut. seismic occurs 23 times in the training tweets and is tied to earthquake reports; the keyword itself is a coin-flip (45 % of the 29 tweets with this keyword are labelled disaster), but the model treats the word as strong evidence.
  2. The counter-evidence was erased by <OOV>. 6 of the 22 tokens (dogger, westward, survey, regent, towing, metre) are unseen or rare in the training tweets and are mapped to the zero <OOV> vector – precisely the words that identify an industrial/maritime context.
  3. Embeddings without world knowledge. The Word2Vec neighbours of seismic (exploration, gabon, somalia, panel…) show that the self-trained space is noisy, and because the embedding is frozen the classifier cannot repair it.
  4. No sentence-level understanding. The bag of surface cues (seismic, coast, cable, area) resembles an official alert; telling an alert from a routine notice needs knowledge the 6,090 training tweets cannot supply.

Error 2 – false negative (id 6552, keyword injury). "My prediction for the Vikings game this Sunday… dont expect a whole lot. Infact I think Zimmer goal is… injury free 1st game" – labelled disaster, predicted non-disaster (P = 0.095 LSTM, 0.173 Simple RNN). Likely reasons:

  1. The model is arguably right and the label is doubtful. The tweet is about an American-football game and wishes for an injury-free game; nothing describes an emergency. Kaggle's labels are crowd-sourced and noisy: 29 of the 294 errors (≈ 10 %) belong to texts that appear elsewhere in the data with both labels (they were excluded from the selection above), and the list of the most confident false negatives is dominated by figurative uses – "the one bleeding", "High School Crush", "traumatised" by a film – labelled disaster.
  2. Keyword ambiguity. injury is a weak cue: only 29 % of the 38 tweets with this keyword are disaster tweets, so a low probability is the statistically sensible output.
  3. Negation and context are invisible to a frozen bag of word vectors. "injury free" contains the disaster word but negates it; with 4 of 23 tokens <OOV> (prediction, vikings, infact, zimmer) the sports context is only partly visible to the network.

Pattern across errors. False negatives (205) outnumber false positives (89) 2.3 : 1. Many of them are figurative or ambiguous uses of disaster words with questionable labels, which puts a ceiling on the achievable score; the genuine model failures (such as error 1) come from missing world knowledge and unseen vocabulary.

Proposed improvement: pre-trained Twitter embeddings (GloVe-Twitter, 100-d) instead of Word2Vec trained on 6,090 tweets¶

Proposal. Keep the architecture, the 100-d size and the frozen-embedding recipe, but initialise the embedding layer from GloVe vectors pre-trained on 2 billion tweets instead of from the Word2Vec model learned on only 82,691 tokens.

Technical justification (each point is backed by evidence earlier in this notebook).

  1. Root cause. Both analysed errors need knowledge the training corpus cannot provide (a "seismic survey" is oil-and-gas exploration; "injury" in a football context is not a disaster). Q3.2 showed that the self-trained space is weak (hand-made groups barely separable, cosines ≤ 0.34, spurious pairs). A classifier on top of a frozen representation can only be as good as that representation, so improving the representation addresses the cause rather than a symptom.
  2. Drop-in change. GloVe-Twitter exists in the same 100 dimensions, so no layer changes; because it was trained on tweets it matches the register (hashtags-as-words, slang, abbreviations).
  3. Coverage. 12.6 % of the test tokens are <OOV> for the self-trained model; GloVe-Twitter covers 96.3 % of them, so the evidence that offsets a misleading keyword (error 1) is no longer erased.
  4. Isolating the mechanism. A control experiment gives the same coverage without outside knowledge: FastText trained on the same tweets can build a vector for any word from its character n-grams (0 % unseen tokens). If coverage alone were the fix, FastText would help – it does not (F1 0.7502 vs 0.7534, McNemar p = 1.0). So the gain has to come from the semantic knowledge distilled from a very large corpus, which is exactly what the proposal adds.

Evidence (same LSTM recipe; test set; the encoding uses surface forms only, no labels).

In [17]:
# Evidence for the proposal: same LSTM recipe, only the embedding changes (Word2Vec -> FastText, also 100-d).
from gensim.models import FastText

t0 = time.time()
ft = FastText(sentences=train_df["tokens"].tolist(), vector_size=W2V_DIM, window=W2V_WINDOW, min_count=W2V_MIN_COUNT,
              sg=1, negative=10, min_n=3, max_n=6, epochs=W2V_EPOCHS, seed=SEED, workers=1, hashfxn=stable_hash)
print(f"FastText trained in {time.time() - t0:.1f}s | in-vocabulary words {len(ft.wv):,}")

# FastText can build a vector for ANY word from its character n-grams, so the embedding table can be extended at
# inference time with the surface forms of new tweets (no labels, no retraining). Rows for the vocabulary below are
# computed from the model trained on the training tweets only.
all_tokens = sorted({w for toks in pd.concat([train_df["tokens"], test_df["tokens"]]) for w in toks})
ft_word2idx = {w: i + 1 for i, w in enumerate(all_tokens)}                    # 0 = <PAD>
ft_matrix = np.zeros((len(all_tokens) + 1, W2V_DIM), dtype="float32")
for w, i in ft_word2idx.items():
    ft_matrix[i] = ft.wv[w]


def ft_encode(token_lists):
    seqs = [[ft_word2idx[w] for w in toks] for toks in token_lists]
    return keras.utils.pad_sequences(seqs, maxlen=MAX_LEN, padding="pre", truncating="post", value=0)


Xft_all, Xft_test = ft_encode(train_df["tokens"]), ft_encode(test_df["tokens"])
ft_data = (Xft_all[tr_idx], y_tr, Xft_all[val_idx], y_val)                      # identical split indices
print(f"Embedding rows: {ft_matrix.shape[0]:,} | test tokens needing <OOV>: 0.0% "
      f"(Word2Vec pipeline: {oov_rate:.1%})")

ft_model, ft_hist, _ = train_model("LSTM", matrix=ft_matrix, data=ft_data, verbose=0)
ft_prob = ft_model.predict(Xft_test, batch_size=256, verbose=0).ravel()
ft_pred = (ft_prob >= 0.5).astype(int)
cmp = pd.DataFrame({
    "LSTM + Word2Vec (main)": {m: results["LSTM"][m] for m in ["Accuracy", "Precision", "Recall", "F1"]},
    "LSTM + FastText (proposal)": dict(Accuracy=accuracy_score(y_test, ft_pred), Precision=precision_score(y_test, ft_pred),
                                       Recall=recall_score(y_test, ft_pred), F1=f1_score(y_test, ft_pred)),
}).T
display(cmp.round(4))
a_ok, b_ok = results["LSTM"]["pred"] == y_test, ft_pred == y_test
bb, cc = int((a_ok & ~b_ok).sum()), int((~a_ok & b_ok).sum())
print(f"Only Word2Vec-LSTM correct: {bb} | only FastText-LSTM correct: {cc} | exact McNemar p = "
      f"{binomtest(bb, bb + cc, 0.5).pvalue:.4f}")

# the two analysed tweets under the proposed model
for name, row in [("ERROR 1 (FP)", fp_row), ("ERROR 2 (FN)", fn_row)]:
    i = test_df.index[test_df["id"] == row["id"]][0]
    print(f"{name}: true={int(row['y_true'])} | P(disaster) Word2Vec-LSTM={results['LSTM']['prob'][i]:.3f} "
          f"-> FastText-LSTM={ft_prob[i]:.3f}")
ft_summary = {k: float(v) for k, v in cmp.loc["LSTM + FastText (proposal)"].items()}
(OUT_DIR / "fasttext_experiment.json").write_text(json.dumps(ft_summary, indent=2))

# Proposal under test: initialise from PRE-TRAINED GloVe-Twitter-100d (2 billion tweets) instead of the 82k-token corpus.
# Same encoding as the FastText run above (vocabulary of surface forms only), same frozen-embedding LSTM recipe.
import contextlib, io
from gensim import downloader as gensim_api

GLOVE_CACHE = OUT_DIR / "glove_experiment.json"
glove_kv = None
try:
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()), contextlib.redirect_stderr(io.StringIO()):   # hide progress bar
        glove_kv = gensim_api.load("glove-twitter-100")
except Exception as exc:
    print(f"Could not obtain glove-twitter-100 ({type(exc).__name__}: {exc}).")

if glove_kv is not None:
    glove_matrix = np.zeros((len(all_tokens) + 1, 100), dtype="float32")
    hit = np.zeros(len(all_tokens) + 1, dtype=bool)
    for w, i in ft_word2idx.items():
        if w in glove_kv:
            glove_matrix[i], hit[i] = glove_kv[w], True
    test_tok = [w for toks in test_df["tokens"] for w in toks]
    cover = np.mean([w in glove_kv for w in test_tok])
    print(f"GloVe-Twitter-100 vocabulary {len(glove_kv):,} words | covers {hit.sum():,}/{len(all_tokens):,} of our word types "
          f"and {cover:.1%} of test tokens (Word2Vec-from-scratch: {1 - oov_rate:.1%})")
    del glove_kv

    gl_model, gl_hist, _ = train_model("LSTM", matrix=glove_matrix, data=ft_data, verbose=0)
    gl_prob = gl_model.predict(Xft_test, batch_size=256, verbose=0).ravel()
    gl_pred = (gl_prob >= 0.5).astype(int)
    row = dict(Accuracy=accuracy_score(y_test, gl_pred), Precision=precision_score(y_test, gl_pred),
               Recall=recall_score(y_test, gl_pred), F1=f1_score(y_test, gl_pred))
    cmp3 = pd.concat([cmp, pd.DataFrame({"LSTM + GloVe-Twitter (proposal)": row}).T])
    display(cmp3.round(4))

    g_ok = gl_pred == y_test
    gb, gc = int((a_ok & ~g_ok).sum()), int((~a_ok & g_ok).sum())
    print(f"Only Word2Vec-LSTM correct: {gb} | only GloVe-LSTM correct: {gc} | exact McNemar p = "
          f"{binomtest(gb, gb + gc, 0.5).pvalue:.4f}")

    # seed robustness for the proposal (same five seeds as before)
    g_rows = []
    for seed in SEEDS:
        m, h, _ = train_model("LSTM", seed=seed, matrix=glove_matrix, data=ft_data, verbose=0)
        pp = (m.predict(Xft_test, batch_size=256, verbose=0).ravel() >= 0.5).astype(int)
        g_rows.append(dict(seed=seed, Accuracy=accuracy_score(y_test, pp), F1=f1_score(y_test, pp)))
    g_df = pd.DataFrame(g_rows)
    base = seed_df[seed_df.model == "LSTM"].set_index("seed")
    print(f"5-seed mean  Accuracy: Word2Vec-LSTM {base.Accuracy.mean():.4f} +- {base.Accuracy.std():.4f} "
          f"vs GloVe-LSTM {g_df.Accuracy.mean():.4f} +- {g_df.Accuracy.std():.4f}")
    print(f"5-seed mean  F1      : Word2Vec-LSTM {base.F1.mean():.4f} +- {base.F1.std():.4f} "
          f"vs GloVe-LSTM {g_df.F1.mean():.4f} +- {g_df.F1.std():.4f}  "
          f"(GloVe better in {(g_df.set_index('seed').F1 > base.F1).sum()} of {len(SEEDS)} seeds)")

    for name, r in [("ERROR 1 (FP)", fp_row), ("ERROR 2 (FN)", fn_row)]:
        i = test_df.index[test_df["id"] == r["id"]][0]
        print(f"{name}: true={int(r['y_true'])} | P(disaster) Word2Vec-LSTM={results['LSTM']['prob'][i]:.3f} "
              f"-> GloVe-LSTM={gl_prob[i]:.3f}")
    GLOVE_CACHE.write_text(json.dumps({**{k: float(v) for k, v in row.items()},
                                       "seed_mean_accuracy": float(g_df.Accuracy.mean()),
                                       "seed_mean_f1": float(g_df.F1.mean())}, indent=2))
elif GLOVE_CACHE.exists():
    print("Offline: showing the cached result of the GloVe experiment from the original run:")
    print(GLOVE_CACHE.read_text())
else:
    print("GloVe experiment skipped (no network and no cached result).")

5-seed mean  Accuracy: Word2Vec-LSTM 0.7886 +- 0.0111 vs GloVe-LSTM 0.8146 +- 0.0102
5-seed mean  F1      : Word2Vec-LSTM 0.7132 +- 0.0310 vs GloVe-LSTM 0.7735 +- 0.0058  (GloVe better in 5 of 5 seeds)

ERROR 2 (FN): true=1 | P(disaster) Word2Vec-LSTM=0.095 -> GloVe-LSTM=0.124

Result. With GloVe-Twitter the LSTM improves on every aggregate metric of the single seed-42 run: accuracy 0.8070 → 0.8234, precision 0.8346 → 0.8481, recall 0.6865 → 0.7171 and F1 0.7534 → 0.7771. The improvement is not a lucky seed: over the five extra seeds the mean F1 is 0.7735 ± 0.0058 vs 0.7132 ± 0.0310 and the mean accuracy 0.8146 vs 0.7886; GloVe wins in 5 of 5 seeds and is also much more stable across seeds. For the single seed-42 comparison the exact McNemar test gives p = 0.074 – suggestive rather than conclusive on its own, but consistent with the five-seed evidence. FastText, as predicted by the analysis, gives no gain.

Honest limits. (i) The two analysed tweets are still misclassified (error 1: P(disaster) 0.990 → 0.913; error 2: 0.095 → 0.124) – the proposal raises recall overall but does not remove label noise or the keyword shortcut entirely, which would need contextual models (a fine-tuned BiLSTM/attention model or BERT) or cleaner labels. (ii) GloVe uses external data, so it is reported as an improvement experiment only; the graded comparison in Q3.1–Q3.4 uses the task-mandated self-trained Word2Vec. (iii) The result is from one dataset split.
